statements.quote: The transformer you have been building all this chapter passes every token through every weight: one dense feed-forward block per layer, and that block is the bulk of the model's parameters.
That means the model's **capacity** (how many parameters it stores) and its **compute per token** (how many it actually uses) are the same number — you cannot have one without the other.
**Mixture of Experts (MoE)** breaks that lock.

It lets a model *store* a very large number of parameters while *activating* only a small fraction for each token — so you get the knowledge of a 600-billion-parameter model at the speed and cost of a 30-billion one.

By 2026 this is not a niche trick; it is how most frontier models are built (\cite[Jiang et al., 2024]{mixtral2024}; \cite[DeepSeek-V3, 2024]{deepseekv3tech2024}), and it is the single most important reason the "size of a model" question has quietly become two questions: *total* and *active*.

blocks.quote: A cleaner decomposition arrived with DeepSeekMoE (\cite[DeepSeekMoE, 2024]{deepseekmoe2024}) and was carried into DeepSeek-V3 (\cite[DeepSeek-V3, 2024]{deepseekv3tech2024}); the design is now the reference. The first is a **shared expert**: one expert is *dense* — every token goes through it — while the remaining experts are *sparse* — routed as usual. The shared expert holds the knowledge that *every* token needs (syntax, general language form), and the routed experts hold the *specialized* knowledge (a domain, a rare pattern). It is a clean split: "what everyone shares" + "what this token picks." The second idea, **auxiliary-loss-free balancing**, replaces the fixed aux penalty with a *dynamic* router whose bias grows for under-used experts and shrinks for over-used ones, so the routing self-corrects during training rather than being tugged by a separate term — reported to give a stable run at 671 billion parameters with no irrecoverable loss spikes \cite[DeepSeek-V3 (2024)]{deepseekv3tech2024}.
blocks.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

blocks.quote: DeepSeekMoE made the expert bank finer and split off the part every token needs. It segments each expert into smaller pieces, so a token can combine several narrow specialists instead of one broad FFN, and it isolates a **shared expert** that every token passes through (\cite[DeepSeekMoE, 2024]{deepseekmoe2024}). The shared expert carries common syntax and language structure; the routed experts are free to specialize. DeepSeek-V3 keeps this design and adds auxiliary-loss-free balancing, where a per-expert bias — not an extra loss term — is adjusted during training to keep the load even (\cite[Wang et al., 2024]{wang2024auxfree}).

blocks.quote: Mixtral made the arithmetic public. Each layer has eight experts and routes each token to two of them, so the model stores 47 billion parameters but computes with about 13 billion per token (\cite[Jiang et al., 2024]{mixtral2024}). The saving is real but narrower than the name suggests: every expert must still be resident in memory, and the all-to-all that gathers a token's two experts is a latency cost a dense model does not pay. Mixtral's routing analysis also found no clean domain split — the gate follows surface and positional patterns more than topics — which is the empirical corrective to the "grammar expert, code expert" story.

blocks.quote: This is exactly the knob the later chapters turn. The [economic layer](ai_economics) prices a model by its *active* parameters per token, and [Inference vs Training](inference_vs_training.php) shows why the serving cost follows the cache and the active compute, not the total weights. MoE is the cleanest example in this course of a **displaced prerequisite**: the "which part of the machine handles this" question was solved long ago, in the brain (different neurons fire for different inputs) and in the switchboard of a telephone exchange. The transformer did not invent sparsity; it finally made a *learned router* of it.
